newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MALAN WITNESSES LIED TO AVOID CHARGES - DEFENCE.
newsitem.headline: MALAN WITNESSES LIED TO AVOID CHARGES - DEFENCE.

text.p: Three state witnesses falsely identified six black policemen accused of the 1987 massacre of 13 people to save their own skins, the murder trial of South Africa's top security chiefs heard on Friday.

The first of seven defence teams summing up in the trial said three witnesses, Johan Opperman, Alex Khumalo and Andre Cloete, who gave evidence in return for indemnity for the role they played in the killings, were unreliable witnesses.

"They had to give evidence implicating some people in order to become state witnesses and to escape the prospects of long terms of imprisonment which would clearly and certainly be imposed were they to be convicted," defence lawyer Klaus von Lieres said.
"On their own stories they would have been convicted of most serious offences," he added.
Lieres is defending the six policeman at the trial whose most senior defendant is former apartheid defence minister Magnus Malan.

Opperman, a former Military Intelligence (MI) officer, admitted to planning the January 1987 hitsquad attack near the east coast city of Durban in which 13 people, including six children aged between four and 10, were killed.

He outlined the training, arming, funding and deployment of 200-strong paramilitary force of Zulus aligned to the Inkatha Freedom Party by MI as part of a covert government plan to counter black liberation movements.
Malan is on trial with three generals, a vice-admiral, a senior policeman, three military officers, six black policemen and a top Inkatha official.
The men stand accused of 13 charges of murder, attempted murder and conspiracy to murder stemming from the massacre.
Cloete was Opperman's second-in-charge. The state has asked that he not be granted indemnity because of his poor showing while giving evidence.

Khumalo, a member of the paramilitary force, helped gather intelligence before the 10-member hitsquad drawn from the force attacked the home of a youth activist aligned to the African National Congress, the IFP's fiercest rivals.
"The bottom line is that they are unreliable witnesses," Lieres said.

The prosecution has conceded it was unable to prove its case "beyond a reasonable doubt" against two of the six suspended policemen and has asked that they be acquitted of the murder and attempted murder charges.
